    mssrscopR

    mssrscopR computes single-frame Mean-Shift Super-Resolution (MSSR; Torres-García et al. 2022) structure maps in R. Geometry is explicit, degenerate input has a defined result, and a self-test can check any installation.

    • Compute: mssr() returns the MSSR structure map of one 2D frame, with its role, grid transform, parameters and diagnostics.
    • Locate: mssr_coords() places output pixels in input-pixel coordinates.
    • Select: mssr_mask() derives a structural mask on the input grid for measuring the original data, and reports how much of it tie-breaking decided.
    • Verify: mssr_selftest() recomputes bundled synthetic fixtures.

    Status: 0.1.0, experimental. At amplification 1 with intensity normalization off, the engine matches the authors’ single-frame R code (disk kernel, rotation undone) and Python code (square kernel) wherever their output is finite, apart from undefined refinement steps; the bundled synthetic fixtures guard against regressions. Its benefit for fluorescence, histology or hyperspectral analyses has not been established.

    Why

    MSSR is easy to run and easy to misread:

    • The authors’ R script returns a rotated image. It fails on non-square frames and returns NaN for flat input.
    • “Amplification” is ambiguous. It adds samples, not observations, and common interpolation grids shift the field of view.
    • The output looks like an image of intensities, but it is not one. MSSR is nonlinear: dim structures next to bright ones are suppressed, and broad or touching objects can be hollowed or split.

    mssrscopR makes each of these explicit: outputs keep the input orientation, coordinates and the field of view are returned with the result, and every result is labeled as a non-quantitative structure map.

    Scope

    In scope

    • Single-frame MSSR of finite 2D numeric matrices of any shape, orders 0–10, integer amplification 1–64 on a field-of-view-preserving grid.
    • Defined results for degenerate input (flat frames, impulses on an exactly zero background), reported in the diagnostics.
    • Structural masks with exact coverage for measurements on the original data.
    • Input validation with classed errors and warnings, resource guards, and an installation self-test.

    Out of scope

    • Temporal MSSR summaries over frame stacks (mean, variance, TPM).
    • Tiled or out-of-core processing: every order step uses image-wide maxima.
    • File readers, physical calibration, and claims of resolution gain, intensity fidelity or diagnostic value.

    Where it sits in CTTIR 

    2D frame from any reader (one channel / one band at a time)
      │
      ▼
mssrscopR::mssr()  →  structure map + coordinates + diagnostics
      │
      ▼
mssrscopR::mssr_mask()  →  mask on the input grid
      │
      ▼
measurements on the ORIGINAL frame (your analysis code)

    There are no adapters to other CTTIR packages yet. Use with hyperspectral cubes or segmentation workflows has not been validated.

    Interface

    Function Returns
    mssr(x, fwhm, amp = 1, order = 1, ...) mssr_result: values, role, transform, parameters, engine, diagnostics
    mssr_coords(result) output pixel-center coordinates (row, col) in input-pixel units
    mssr_mask(result, fraction = 0.5, region = NULL, seed = 1) logical mask on the input grid with coverage, tie_fraction, n_region
    mssr_selftest(tolerance = 1e-10) fixture errors, with attribute all_passed
    mssr_app(max_upload_mb = 50, ...) interactive Shiny explorer (needs shiny, bslib and jsonlite): synthetic examples or an uploaded frame, maps on shared input-pixel axes, profiles, masks measured on the input, self-test, downloads

    fwhm is the point-spread-function width in input pixels and has no default. Errors inherit from mssrscopR_error (subclasses _input, _nonfinite, _parameter, _resource, _unsupported, _numerical, _dependency); negative input gives a mssrscopR_warning_negative warning, because MSSR assumes non-negative intensities, and undefined refinement steps give a mssrscopR_warning_skipped_steps warning.

    Use plain integer or double inputs; explicitly classed numeric objects must be converted deliberately. Intermediate overflow raises a numerical error. Coordinate and mask consumers check finite values and consistent grid metadata; they do not authenticate image provenance. Positive mask fractions select at least one pixel, but flat maps may yield entirely tie-selected masks. A quota mask is not a cell segmentation.

    Installation 

    # install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("CTTIR/mssrscopR")

    Quick start 

    library(mssrscopR)

# Two blurred point sources 3 pixels apart (FWHM 3 px) on a faint background:
# a shallow dip in the input that MSSR deepens.
g <- expand.grid(r = 1:21, c = 1:25)
spot <- function(r0, c0) exp(-((g$r - r0)^2 + (g$c - c0)^2) / (2 * (3 / 2.3548)^2))
x <- matrix(spot(11, 11) + spot(11, 14) + 0.05, 21, 25)

res <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
res
mssr_coords(res)$col[1:4]

m <- mssr_mask(mssr(x, fwhm = 3), fraction = 0.25)
mean(x[m])                       # measured on the original frame
attr(m, "tie_fraction")

attr(mssr_selftest(), "all_passed")

# Explore parameters interactively (needs shiny, bslib and jsonlite):
# mssr_app()

    Relation to the authors’ code

    The authors distribute R, Python, MATLAB and ImageJ code at https://github.com/adanog/MSSR. mssrscopR is an independent implementation and contains none of it. At amplification 1 with intensity normalization off, its output equals the authors’ single-frame R function once that function’s final rotation is undone, and with kernel = "square" their Python function, wherever their code returns finite values. For flat frames and for impulses on an exactly zero background their R function returns NaN and their Python function returns zeros; mssrscopR returns flagged zeros for flat frames and keeps the map, counting the skipped step, for impulses. With intensity normalization on, their R function multiplies the rotated map by the unrotated input, so it matches mssr() only for frames that a 90-degree rotation leaves unchanged (and fails for non-square frames). Their R mesh compensation shifts asymmetrically (by desp + 1 one way and desp the other); mssrscopR uses the symmetric shifts of their Python code. Amplification uses Keys cubic convolution on a field-of-view-preserving grid, so output for amp > 1 differs from the authors’ interpolation.

    Citation

    Please cite the method paper whenever you use MSSR; citation("mssrscopR") lists it together with the package.

    Torres-García E, Pinto-Cámara R, Linares A, et al. Extending resolution within a single imaging frame. Nature Communications 2022;13:7452. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-34693-9

    Use of LLM tools

    Where applicable, LLM tools were used for narrowly defined, non-authorial tasks: copyediting, prose refinement, Markdown/LaTeX formatting, boilerplate scaffolding (such as CI configurations and build scripts), and code refactoring. Tools included Chat AI, the KISSKI (GWDG) service, and self-hosted Mistral Small (24B, Apache-2.0) served through a local vLLM architecture on an Ubuntu Linux workstation with Intel processors and NVIDIA GPUs. The self-hosted model ran locally, with no data sent to third parties.

    All scientific claims, methodological choices, analyses, interpretations and conclusions remain the authors’ own. Where applicable, LLM-generated material must be reviewed and revised before inclusion, and references must be verified against their DOI, arXiv ID or ISBN.

    Local software setup: vLLM with Python/PyTorch, plus R and RStudio.
